title: API failure cookbook & mitigation sketch
body:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight "cookbook" for on-call engineers and incident reviewers to quickly choose pragmatic mitigations for common API failures: request timeouts, client 429s, degraded streaming, and elevated error rates. Meant as a living sketch — contains short-term surgical actions (what to flip now), medium-term containment, and notes for post-incident follow-up.

Scope / audience:
- Eng-SRE responders during first 30–120 minutes of an incident
- Incident reviewers building runbooks and runbook tests
- Solutions engineers who want standard mitigations to recommend to customers

TL;DR quick checklist (first 8 minutes)
1) Confirm alerts and scope: open Datadog/Prometheus dashboard + PagerDuty incident.
2) Identify symptom bucket: timeouts | 429s (client throttling) | streaming degradation | elevated 5xx.
3) If broad impact and rising severity: enable global fallback routing to lower-tier model variant (if available).
4) If bursting latency on specific nodes: cordon/evict suspects and scale up dedicated pool or enable burst-capacity.
5) Communicate brief status to #oncall and incident channel (one-line, impact, action).

How to decide the symptom bucket quickly
- Timeouts: 95th percentile request latency > SLO and many streaming keepalive disconnects. Check: latency heatmap and server-side request_duration histogram.
- 429s: client-facing 429 spike with x-rate-limit headers present, origin shows rejected queue length.
- Degraded streaming: clients receive partial or stalled chunks; server logs show send() stalls or work-queue backlog in streamer workers.
- Elevated error rates: sudden jump in 5xx ratio or model runtime exceptions in logs.

Common mitigation patterns (ranked by speed / invasiveness)
1) Traffic shaping and routing
- Quick: apply coarse global countermeasure: route a % of traffic to a cheaper, lower-latency model variant or warm fallback API endpoints.
- How: Console -> Routes -> Create weighted split (e.g., 20% fallback). In infra: update envoy route weights or feature-flag.
- When to use: broad client 429s or model-level saturation.
2) Rate-limiting relax & backoff tuning
- Quick: temporarily raise internal rate-limit thresholds for high-tier customers, or disable server-side strict per-IP rate-limit for 10–30 minutes.
- How: patch rate-limit config (ConfigMap/feature flag), verify using traffic logs.
- Risk: may elevate load; combine with capacity scaling if you relax limits.
3) Autoscale / capacity changes
- Quick: trigger manual scale (increase replica count, add GPU pool) if autoscale is slow.
- How: kubectl scale deployment/model-serving --replicas=N OR toggle burst-capacity.
- When: localized node saturation, GPU queue length high, or sustained queue growth.
4) Caching / KV prefix warmup
- Quick: enable prefix caching for high-frequency prompts (if available) or enable response cache TTL extension.
- How: flip caching flag and seed cache with synthetic common prefixes.
5) Circuit breaker and graceful degradation
- Quick: lower max concurrency per model worker or enable graceful failure mode that returns cached or truncated responses.
- Why: reduces tail latency and keeps some clients served.
6) Rollback recent deploys / config changes
- Quick: if incident correlates with a rollout, revert to last known good revision.
- How: Console -> Rollouts -> Rollback, or kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>.

Detailed per-failure recipes
A) Timeouts (client-visible 502/504 / streaming stalls)
Detection:
- Server-side p50-p99 latency spike, worker queue length rising; traces show long model inference time or blocked I/O.
Immediate actions (0–15m):
- Switch small % of traffic to lower-cost variant to relieve overloaded model pool.
- If tail latency originates from specific nodes: drain/cordon them and spin new nodes.
- Check for hot shards in KV cache and restart offending cache processes.
Commands & checks:
- datadog: query APM traces for service:inference AND http.status_code:[502 TO 504]
- kubectl get pods -o wide --selector=app=model-serving
- curl -v https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health -> check internal latency header X-Internal-Latency
Medium term (15m–3h):
- Scale dedicated GPU pool or enable burst capacity.
- Patch runtime to cap per-request memory and fail fast on out-of-memory.
Post-incident:
- Add synthetic slow-path tests to CI, increase telemetry around model run loop and kernel queue times.

B) 429s (client throttles)
Detection:
- Spike in 429 responses with X-RateLimit-* headers, origin logs show reject count. Correlates with ingress rate limiter metrics.
Immediate actions (0–10m):
- Temporarily relax enforcement level for known internal/partner API keys (increase quota).
- If caused by a customer ramp: contact customer success for coordinated throttling or ask them to reduce rate.
- Deploy a short-lived token bucket refresh to accept queued requests instead of rejecting outright.
Commands & checks:
- dd: metric rate_limiter.reject_count by rule
- check ingress logs for top-URL and top-api-key
Medium term (10m–2h):
- Increase capacity for rate-limiter components and tune burst windows.
- Implement softer 202-accepted queued response pattern for low-priority requests.
Post-incident:
- Add a proactive quota-warning webhook to inform customers before hard 429s.

C) Streaming degradation (stalls, truncated streams)
Detection:
- Clients report stalled SSE/websocket streams; server logs show stalled send buffers or long GC pauses.
Immediate actions (0–20m):
- Failover streaming sessions to alternative region or instance group that recently handled streaming traffic.
- If GC is the culprit: temporarily bump heap settings or restart affected pods gradually.
- Switch streaming to chunked polling fallback if available for critical customers.
Commands & checks:
- tail logs for 'write to socket' errors, netstat for COLLOF? (network backlog)
- Console: streaming worker pool utilization graph
Medium term (20m–6h):
- Add backpressure-aware client library updates: reduce default chunk size and add heartbeat.
- Instrument per-connection latency and backlog depth more granularly.
Post-incident:
- Run a chaos test that simulates network stalls to validate streaming fallbacks.

D) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes)
Detection:
- Error budget burn rate high; increase in application 500s; stack traces point to model runtime exceptions, dependency faults, or bad input patterns.
Immediate actions (0–30m):
- Short-circuit inputs with known-bad signatures (sanitize/blacklist) and return a sanitized error message rather than retrying.
- Roll back recent model or infra changes if correlated.
- Enable increased sampling for traces to surface root cause.
Commands & checks:
- search logs for recurring exception message
- check model quantization/weights artifact checksum
Medium term (30m–24h):
- Add input validation layer in the edge gateway to drop malformed requests early.
- Harden model loading paths and add canary tests for new model artifacts.
Post-incident:
- Create an eval set of inputs that triggered the failure and add to model CI.

Communication templates (incident channel snippets)
- Short status update (first post): "INCIDENT: API errors impacting chat endpoints (p95 latency > 2s). Impact: ~22% of requests. Action: routing 20% to fallback variant + manual scale. ETA next update 10m."
- Update (after action): "ACTIONED: routing & scale applied. Error rate down from 22% -> 8% in 6m. Investigating root cause (model queue backlog)."

Escalation matrix / ownership
- If mitigation fails within 30m escalate to oncall-sre-2 and paging eng-product for possible feature-flag rollback.
- If customer-facing SLA at risk, page the customer success lead.

Observability & telemetry to prioritize (Post-incident playbook)
- Add request-level correlation ID to streaming chunks and ensure traces are sampled at 100% for affected endpoints during incidents.
- Emit model internal queue length, kernel-run-queue, and per-request memory usage.
- Track: p50/p95/p99 latency, 429/sec, 5xx/sec, streaming-chunk-latency, queue-depth per-worker.

Runbook TODOs and follow-ups (to convert this sketch into a formal runbook)
- Add explicit CLI commands for common actions (kubectl, envoy/istio route commands, console paths).
- Author verified rollback playbooks per service (who runs what, with exact CLI).
- Create canary tests for streaming fallback and queued acceptance behavior.
- Build automated runbook checks that surface the right mitigation choices in the Console when an alert fires.

Post-incident review prompts (for PIR)
- What mitigations reduced customer impact fastest and why?
- Were we confident in the telemetry to make the routing/rollback decision?
- Which changes (deploys/config) preceded the incident?
- Action items assigned (with owners and due dates).

Appendix: quick commands cheatsheet (examples)
- kubectl get pods -l app=model-serving -o wide
- kubectl cordon <pod> && kubectl drain <pod> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- kubectl scale deploy/model-serving --replicas=10
- curl -sS -D - https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health | grep X-

Notes and provenance:
- Inspired by recent incidents in Q3–Q4 2024 that involved sudden model worker queue saturation and a separate customer-induced 429 spike.
- This doc intentionally uses generic product terms (model variant, streaming worker) so it can apply across Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments.

End of sketch.

Revision history:
- 2024-09-20 initial sketch by Evelyn Brooks
- 2024-11-12 added streaming fallback patterns (Alex Chen)
- 2025-12-05 expanded telemetry checklist and TODOs (Priya Nair)
